proposal.description:
Criterion focus: Evaluates the accuracy and plausibility of semantic labels and contextual inferences derived from visual cues, rather than just the presence of observable elements.

Applicable only when: Candidates differ in their interpretation of visual elements' meaning, function, or context (e.g., labeling text purpose, inferring activity from posture, identifying icons vs. generic shapes).

Not applicable when: Differences are purely about object detection counts, colors, or spatial layout without semantic interpretation, or when inferences are pure hallucinations unrelated to any visual cues.

Decision rule: Prefer the candidate that offers semantically accurate labels and contextually plausible inferences grounded in visual cues. If one candidate makes a reasonable inference (e.g., text function, activity context) supported by visual evidence while the other makes a semantically inaccurate claim (e.g., misidentifying a logo) or forces an unsupported object association to appear grounded, prefer the former. Return None if both offer equally plausible interpretations or if the difference is purely stylistic.
proposal.rationale: This criterion is narrower than the parent because it specifically targets the interpretation of visual details (semantics/context) rather than the mere presence of visual details. It addresses the cluster's shared failure where the parent penalizes valid inferences or accurate semantic labels for not being 'strictly visual' enough, while rewarding literal but semantically inaccurate descriptions. It helps the judge distinguish between grounded inference and hallucination, prioritizing human-aligned understanding over rigid object listing.
